title: Infrastructure Engineering Playbook: GPU Fleet, IaC, CI/CD, and Runbooks
author: Laura Chen
body:
Overview

This playbook consolidates Terraform/IaC guidance, GPU fleet and capacity best practices, cloud accounts and networking conventions, CI/CD and build processes, and operational runbooks maintained by the Infrastructure (eng-infra) team. It is intended as the canonical onboarding and operating guide for engineers who provision, operate, or troubleshoot Redwood's GPU-backed inference infrastructure.

Sections in this document:
1) Ownership and contacts
2) GPU fleet & capacity planning
3) Cloud accounts and networking patterns
4) Terraform / IaC modules and guidelines
5) CI/CD and build pipelines for infra modules
6) Runbooks and playbook procedures
7) Oncall, game-days, and capacity SLOs
8) Related resources and repository links

1) Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: infra-plat-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Team: eng-infra (Platform & GPU Fleet)
- Escalation path: oncall -> infra-tech-lead -> eng-sre -> CTO
- PagerDuty rotation: infra-gpu-team (see /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks for rotation schedule)

2) GPU fleet & capacity planning

Purpose: ensure predictable throughput and cost efficiency for production and staging inference workloads.

Key concepts and definitions:
- Provisioned capacity: GPUs reserved for Dedicated workloads.
- Shared pool: burstable cloud GPU pool used for non-SLA workloads.
- Minimum cushion: capacity buffer expressed in GPU-hours (%) to absorb sudden demand.
- Utilization target: desired steady-state utilization (recommended 55-70% for cost/latency balance).

Capacity targets and SLOs:
- Production p99 token latency SLO: < 250ms for typical 512-token sequences (model dependent).
- Capacity headroom target: 25% cushion above expected 95th percentile load for the coming 72h window.
- Cost objective: target <$0.003 per generated token on average across hosted models (tracked in Cost Dashboards).

Sizing and forecasting steps (quarterly cadence):
1. Pull 90/95/99 traffic percentiles from per-route telemetry (Console -> routing dashboards).
2. Convert request volume to GPU-hours using the model-performance table (see /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite).
3. Add on-call runbook cushion (default +25%) and growth runway (weekly growth factor * 2 weeks).
4. Produce purchase/reserve recommendations for Dedicated pools and right-size shared pool.

Operational practices:
- Autoscaling policies: prefer scheduled scaling for predictable daily patterns; target scaling cooldown 3-8 minutes for GPU-backed groups.
- Preemptible/spot usage: only for non-SLA workloads; subscribe to reclaim webhook and implement fast fallback to other regions/variants.
- Preferred instance types: A100 80GB for large-context high-throughput models; H100 for latency-sensitive low-batch inference; NVIDIA L4 for embeddings/low-cost workloads.

3) Cloud accounts and networking

Account structure:
- Org root -> Production account(s) -> Shared infra account -> Staging / QA accounts -> Sandbox per-team accounts.
- Principle: minimal blast radius and clear network boundaries between prod and non-prod.

VPC and subnet conventions:
- Use dedicated VPCs per environment (prod/staging/sandbox) with standardized CIDR blocks: 10.10.x.0/16 for prod, 10.20.x.0/16 for staging.
- Use public/private subnets pattern: private subnets host GPU instances, public subnets for NAT gateways and bastions.

Peering and transit networking:
- Transit VPC for shared services (logging, monitoring, build caches). Use VPC Transit Gateway where available.
- Avoid cross-account peering for production GW paths; prefer Transit Gateway + explicit route tables.

Security controls:
- Private GPU instances must not have public IPs; egress via NAT or egress-only gateways.
- Host-based firewall rules enforced via security groups: only allow SSH from bastion security group and metrics/agent ports from monitoring accounts.
- KMS: use customer-managed KMS keys for any customer data-at-rest in private deployments.

4) Terraform / IaC modules and guidelines

Repository layout and module responsibilities:
- github.com/redwood/infra-modules (root) — reusable modules: vpc, subnets, transit-gateway, gpu-node-pool, iam-roles, k8s-cluster, ci-cd-helpers.
- github.com/redwood/infra-environments — environment-level stacks that compose modules for prod/staging/sandbox.

Naming and tagging standards:
- Resource names: <env>-<service>-<region>-<resource> (e.g., prod-inference-us-west1-gpu-pool).
- Tags: owner, cost-center, project, environment, sla-tier, git-commit/version.

Module design guidelines:
- Inputs: explicit, validated (use variable descriptions and validation blocks).
- Outputs: minimal, stable names for other stacks to reference (avoid returning sensitive values).
- Idempotency: modules must be safe to run multiple times; avoid non-deterministic naming.
- Versioning: modules are versioned semantically; environments pin to module versions via git tags or registry releases.

Migration and change procedure for critical modules:
1. Draft RFC/ADR for the change and add to /confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records.
2. Create a branch and unit tests for the module change (see module test harness in infra-modules/test).
3. Run module integration tests in a sandbox environment using the CI pipeline.
4. Coordinate a maintenance window for infra-owner reviewers; apply with small batch incremental rollouts using canary stacks.

5) CI/CD and build pipelines for infra modules

Pipeline overview:
- Source: GitHub mainline with protected branches and codeowners.
- PR checks: terraform fmt, tflint, unit tests (terratest), static security scans (tfsec), policy checks (OPA/Conftest).
- Merge gates: require 2 reviewers and green CI.
- Deployment: pipelines use ephemeral CI runners with credentials retrieved from CI secrets manager; apply steps run under short-lived service accounts.

Example pipeline stages (github actions / buildkite):
1. fmt & lint
2. unit tests (terratest or go/py tests)
3. policy & security scans
4. plan — publish plan artifact
5. approval gate (for module or env-level changes)
6. apply — run terraform apply in targeted mode (or full apply for env stacks)

CI secrets and credentials handling:
- Use vault for secrets; CI obtains ephemeral tokens via OIDC where possible.
- Long-lived credentials are forbidden in CI. Any exceptions require security review and rotation schedule.

Rollback and safety patterns:
- Always commit state backup before destructive changes.
- Use terraform state locking (remote state with DynamoDB or equivalent).
- For critical infra changes, use feature-flagged rollouts and blue/green + canary patterns when possible.

6) Runbooks and playbook procedures

This section contains abbreviated runbooks — full runbooks live under /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks. Each runbook includes owner, run steps, quick diagnostics, and rollback options.

Runbook: GPU node degraded / kernel panic
- Symptoms: node reporting as unhealthy in cluster autoscaler; monitoring alert: gpu-node.*.hostdown.
- Immediate steps:
  1) Identify node in cloud console: aws/ec2 or gcp/compute instance id.
  2) SSH into bastion -> jump to node in private network using session manager.
  3) Collect diagnostics: dmesg, journalctl -u nvidia-container-runtime, /var/log/syslog.
  4) If kernel panic confirmed, cordon & drain node from k8s and create replacement using node-pool autoscaling.
  5) If replacement fails, scale up spare pool in another AZ or fall back to L4/CPU node pool for non-SLA traffic.
  6) Post-incident: file incident report, include heap of logs and root cause analysis, and attach to postmortem.

Runbook: Terraform plan shows unexpected resource deletion
- Symptoms: terraform plan contains deletion of non-intentional resources.
- Immediate steps:
  1) Abort the apply.
  2) Identify the resource and check recent changes to module inputs/versions.
  3) Restore the previous state file snapshot if deletion is unsafe (s3 state backups have hourly snapshots).
  4) Re-run plan after reverting module changes or adjusting inputs.
  5) If apply must proceed, coordinate a maintenance window and notify stakeholders.

7) Oncall, game-days, and capacity SLOs

- Oncall responsibilities: infrastructure oncall is responsible for paging for infra-related incidents and owning the initial triage for GPU capacity alerts, network outages, and terraform apply failures.
- Game-day cadence: quarterly game-days that simulate capacity spikes, region failovers, and reclaiming spot capacity; results documented in eng-platform/retrospectives.
- Capacity SLOs to monitor: utilization targets, queue lengths for inference jobs, and autoscaler scaling latency.

8) Related resources and repository links

- infra-modules repo: https://github.com/redwood/infra-modules
- infra-environments repo: https://github.com/redwood/infra-environments
- GPU runbooks: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026
- Benchmarking: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite
- ADRs: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records

Appendix: Useful CLI snippets

- Terraform plan with targeted apply preview:
  terraform plan -target=module.gpu_node_pool -var-file=env/prod.tfvars

- Check GPU node memory usage (via ssh to node):
  nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.total,memory.used,temperature.gpu --format=csv

- Emergency scale up (one-off):
  aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name prod-gpu-asg --desired-capacity 10

Maintenance and updates

This document is reviewed quarterly and after every major incident affecting GPU capacity or IaC pipelines. To propose edits, open a PR against this page's source in the docs repo and request review from the infra-tech-leads.
